KEY MESSAGE 1...Periodic showers expected in portions of Central NY through
this early evening.

Aloft, cyclonic WNW'erly flow and embedded shortwave troughs
affect Western and Central NY the rest of today. At the surface,
a high pressure ridge continues to build from the western Great
Lakes. Late afternoon highs are expected to reach the mid 50's
to mid 60's, with the coolest readings expected on the Tug Hill
Plateau and in the higher terrain of the western Adirondacks.
Mainly fair weather is expected. However, a few lake-effect rain
showers remain possible over and downwind of Lake America amidst
W'erly to WNW'erly mean low-level flow, 850 mb temperatures near
4C over/downwind of the ~17C lake, and sufficient synoptic-scale
low-level moisture. Even so, latest trends in satellite imagery
suggest sufficient daytime heating of surrounding land and 
overlying air is preventing the lake from being the primary 
source of heat and moisture (i.e. instability), and the 
generation of additional lake-effect rain showers, respectively.
Periodic general rain showers are expected to impact North-Central
NY this afternoon through early evening, as weak boundary layer
CAPE, stemming from daytime warming amidst the sufficient low-level
moisture, should be released by low-level convergence/moist 
ascent along a surface trough axis attendant to a stronger 
shortwave trough embedded in the WNW'erly flow aloft. The 
general showers and any lake-effect showers are expected to end 
by sunset this evening, as the boundary layer stabilizes via 
nocturnal cooling and lake-induced CAPE wanes via synoptic-scale
low-level dry air advection and a lowering subsidence inversion
that will accompany the aforementioned surface ridge.

Dry weather is expected tonight through Saturday as the ridge 
at the surface and then aloft continues to build and then crests
E'ward across our CWA and vicinity, and is accompanied by 
stabilizing subsidence. Despite the development of weak net low-
level WAA on the backside of the surface ridge, mainly clear 
sky, weak surface winds, and low humidity should allow overnight
lows to reach the lower 30's to lower 40's around daybreak
Saturday. The coldest lows are expected in Lewis County. 
Strengthening net low-level WAA and daytime heating should allow
late afternoon highs to reach the upper 50's to mid 60's in 
North-Central NY and the mid 60's to lower 70's elsewhere in 
our CWA.

KEY MESSAGE 2...The remnants of Hurricane Isaias will bring a soaking rain 
to the region overnight Saturday night through Monday morning.

The ridging at the surface and aloft should exit slowly E'ward 
from Western and Central NY as Isaias' remnant and vertically- 
stacked low at the surface and aloft, embedded in a trough 
aloft, wobbles NNE'ward across the TN Valley and toward the 
Lower OH Valley Saturday night. Isolated rain showers are 
possible after midnight and outside of North-Central NY in our 
CWA, in response to moist isentropic ascent aloft generated by 
the low pressure system. Continued net low-level WAA and 
increasing cloud cover will limit nocturnal cooling. Lows should
reach the 40's to mid 50's around daybreak Sunday. On Sunday, 
the ridge at the surface and aloft should continue to exit 
slowly E'ward from our CWA as the aforementioned and vertically-
stacked low at the surface and aloft wobbles NE'ward from near 
the Lower OH Valley toward the central Appalachians and the 
trough axis aloft approaches our CWA from the western Great 
Lakes and vicinity. Widespread rain, steady to heavy at times, 
will continue to overspread our CWA generally from south to 
north as isentropic ascent aloft continues over our region and 
taps into abundant moisture originating over the southern Gulf 
Stream. Despite continued net low-level WAA, abundant cloud 
cover and the wet-bulb effect will limit daytime highs to the 
mid 50's to mid 60's.

During Sunday night through nightfall Monday evening, the trough
axis aloft should move from the central Great Lakes and central
Appalachians toward the Canadian Maritimes and Atlantic waters
east of the Delmarva Peninsula. The vertically-stacked surface
low should dissipate in vicinity of the Mid OH Valley Sunday
night. As the Sunday night through Monday period elapses, the 
low aloft should move generally E'ward from the central
Appalachians toward Atlantic waters east of the Delmarva 
Peninsula and a new surface low should develop, deepen, and 
wobble NE'ward from the Mid-Atlantic states toward Atlantic 
waters south of Nova Scotia, in response to mid/upper-level 
divergence, attendant large-scale tropospheric ascent, and MSLP
falls ahead of the trough axis aloft. Simultaneously, another 
ridge at the surface and aloft should build into our CWA from 
the western Great Lakes and vicinity. Accordingly, the moist 
isentropic ascent over our region should weaken and the related 
rain should taper and then end generally from west to east 
across our area Sunday night through Monday
